instructions: Each child picks a sock and decides their character: hero, monster, animal, grandma.
Glue on googly eyes, yarn hair, and a mouth made from a folded felt oval or a drawn-on smile.
Add personality: ears from felt triangles, a pom-pom nose, a cape from a fabric scrap.
Let glue dry 15 minutes while kids name their puppets and invent one catchphrase each.
Puppet show time: set up a table 'stage,' hide behind it, and perform 2-minute scenes in pairs. Applaud everything.
summary: Turn stray socks into a cast of characters, then put on a full puppet show behind a table stage.
tips: Fabric glue beats hot glue for little hands. Ask families for sock donations a week ahead — you'll always be short.
title: Sock Puppet Workshop

instructions: Cut 3 strands of embroidery floss, each about 24 inches long. Knot them together at the top and tape the knot to the table.
Teach the basic forward knot: make a '4' shape with the left strand over the middle, pull through, repeat twice, then switch sides.
Work down about 5 inches, keeping knots snug but not death-grip tight.
Rule of the session: you must make TWO — one to keep, one to give to someone in the group today.
End with a bracelet exchange circle. Giving away the thing you just worked hard on is the whole lesson.
summary: Learn the classic knotted bracelet — then make two, keep one, and give one away before the day ends.
tips: Start with 3-strand candy-stripe bracelets; the chevron pattern can wait for session two. Pre-cut floss saves 10 minutes.
title: Friendship Bracelets

instructions: Set out stacks of old magazines, catalogs, and newspapers. Give everyone 5 minutes to flip and tear out anything that catches their eye — no plan yet.
Ask a prompt: 'Make a board that shows your perfect weekend,' or 'your dream room,' or 'things that make you laugh.'
Arrange the cutouts on cardstock before gluing — composition first, commitment second.
Glue everything down, overlapping edges. Add doodles, captions, and stickers to tie it together.
Gallery walk: everyone tours the boards. Each artist explains one choice they made.
summary: Tear, arrange, and glue magazine images into personal vision boards — then explain your choices on a gallery walk.
tips: Ask the school library for weeded magazines — they're usually thrilled to offload them. The 'arrange before gluing' rule prevents heartbreak.
title: Magazine Collage Boards

instructions: Wash and dry smooth, flat rocks — palm-sized is ideal.
Paint a base coat if you want, or work directly on the stone. Paint pens give the cleanest lines.
Each rock gets a kind word, a small picture, or both: 'you matter,' a sun, a heart.
Seal with clear acrylic spray (adult job, outside) so the art survives weather.
Hide the finished rocks around the campus or neighborhood for strangers to find. Never sign them — the mystery is the magic.
summary: Paint kind messages on rocks and hide them around campus for strangers to discover — anonymous art with a mission.
tips: The flatter the rock, the happier the painter. Landscaping supply stores sell bags of smooth river rocks cheap.
title: Kindness Rock Painting

instructions: Hold a paper plate up to your face and mark where your eyes are, then cut out two eye holes.
Cut the plate into the mask's basic shape: round it for animals, point the top for cats, add ears.
Paint or color the base, then glue on extras: yarn hair, feather ears, a pom-pom nose.
Poke a small hole on each side and thread elastic through for wearing.
Mask parade: everyone introduces their character in a silly voice before the masks come off.
summary: Cut, paint, and decorate paper plates into wearable animal and character masks — then parade them in silly voices.
tips: Cut eye holes generously — kids always cut them too small. Pre-punch the elastic holes with a hole punch.
title: Paper Plate Masks

instructions: Split into teams of 3–4. Each team claims a table as their city block.
Assign building types: every team must build at least one house, one shop, and one landmark — everything else is free choice.
Build with boxes, tubes, and tape. Cut windows and doors, draw brick patterns, add paper roofs.
Connect the blocks: teams negotiate where roads, bridges, and parks go between their tables.
City tour: each team presents their block. Vote on awards — tallest building, funniest shop name, best park.
summary: Teams of engineers build a cardboard metropolis — houses, shops, landmarks — then connect their blocks into one city.
tips: Collect boxes for two weeks beforehand; you'll need more than you think. Box cutters are adult-only tools, always.
title: Cardboard Box City

instructions: Cut a simple shape from cardboard — a heart, star, initial letter, or animal silhouette.
Tape the end of a yarn strand to the back and start wrapping: crisscross, spiral, or random — there are no wrong answers.
Change colors by tying on a new strand and tucking the knot underneath.
Wrap until the cardboard barely shows through. Trim the tail and tape it down.
Poke a hole, add a string hanger, and display. These make great gifts.
summary: Wrap cardboard shapes in colorful yarn until they become textured art pieces — simple, satisfying, and giftable.
tips: Thick, chunky yarn covers faster and frustrates less. Initial letters are the most popular shape by far.
title: Yarn-Wrapped Art

instructions: Start with a square of origami paper, colored side down. Fold in half, unfold, fold in half the other way — crease everything sharply.
Fold the top corners to the center to make a triangle, then fold the triangle's bottom corners up to the top point.
Flip over and fold the side corners into the center line. Fold the bottom point up, then fold it back down halfway to make the springy 'legs.'
Press all creases hard — sharp folds are what make frogs jump.
Frog races: line them up and press the back to make them hop. Measure whose frog jumps farthest and redesign for distance.
summary: Fold paper frogs that actually hop when you press their backs — then race them and engineer for distance.
tips: Do the first fold along with the group, step by step — origami fails when kids get ahead. Bigger paper (6 inch) is easier than small.
title: Origami Jumping Frogs

instructions: Set up a card station with folded cardstock, markers, stickers, and stamps — leave it running as an ongoing center.
Teach the formula for a great card: a picture on the front, a specific message inside, and a decorated envelope.
Pick a weekly mission: thank-you cards for school staff, birthday cards for classmates, welcome cards for new students.
Collect finished cards in a 'mailbox' and deliver them every Friday.
Track who you've thanked — the goal is to reach every adult in the building by year's end.
summary: Run a permanent card-making station with weekly missions — thank-yous, birthdays, welcomes — delivered every Friday.
tips: Keep it as an always-available station, not a one-time activity. Kids return to it during every free moment once it exists.
title: Card-Making Station

instructions: Bend a chenille stem or thin wire into a circle about 4 inches across and twist the ends together.
Tie yarn to the circle and wrap it all the way around until the frame is fully covered.
Tie a new strand and weave a web: loop around the frame, then loop each new stitch through the previous loop, spiraling inward.
Leave a small hole in the center. Tie on 3 strands hanging down and thread beads and feathers onto them.
Hang near a window. Share the Ojibwe origin story of dream catchers respectfully — this is a real cultural tradition, not just a craft.
summary: Weave yarn webs on wire hoops with beaded hangers — and learn the real cultural story behind the craft.
tips: This one needs patience — best for ages 8+. Tell the origin story first; kids weave more carefully when they know what it means.
title: Yarn Dream Catchers

instructions: Build the volcano: mound modeling clay or a dirt pile around a small plastic cup, leaving the cup's mouth open at the top.
Spoon 2 tablespoons of baking soda into the cup. Add a squirt of dish soap and a few drops of red food coloring.
Gather the group around. Ask for predictions: what will happen when we add the 'lava starter'?
Pour in 1/4 cup of vinegar and step back. The fizzing eruption overflows the crater.
Run it again with a twist: more vinegar? Less baking soda? Warm vs. cold vinegar? Record which combo erupts biggest.
summary: The classic chemical eruption — baking soda meets vinegar in a clay crater — then experiment with the recipe.
tips: Always use a tray. Always. The second round of experiments is where the actual science learning happens, so don't skip it.
title: Baking Soda Volcanoes

instructions: Split into teams of 3–4. Each team gets 20 marshmallows and 20 pieces of dry spaghetti.
Challenge: build the tallest freestanding tower in 15 minutes. It must stand alone for 10 seconds to count.
No eating the building materials until judging is done. (This rule will be tested.)
Measure every tower. Winning team explains their design: wide base? triangles? cross-bracing?
Rebuild round: teams get 5 minutes to improve using what they learned from the winners.
summary: Twenty marshmallows, twenty spaghetti sticks, fifteen minutes — build the tallest freestanding tower you can.
tips: Stale marshmallows are actually stickier and work better. Triangles beat squares every time — let kids discover it.
title: Marshmallow Tower Challenge

instructions: Give each builder 5 sheets of paper and 12 inches of tape. The challenge: span a 12-inch gap between two stacks of books.
Test each bridge by stacking pennies in the center until it collapses. Record the weight held.
Rebuild round: same materials, but now builders can fold, roll, or accordion the paper first.
Test again. Almost every bridge holds dramatically more — folded paper is corrugated, like real bridge beams.
Discuss: which shapes held most? Where did bridges fail? That's exactly how engineers talk.
summary: Engineer a paper bridge across a book canyon, load it with pennies until it fails, then redesign and retest.
tips: Accordion folds are the secret weapon. Let kids test-destroy freely — failure data is the best data.
title: Paper Bridge Engineering

instructions: Fill a clear bottle one-third full with water, then add vegetable oil until nearly full. Let it settle — the layers separate.
Add 8–10 drops of food coloring. Watch them sink through the oil and burst into the water layer.
Drop in half an Alka-Seltzer tablet and watch: blobs of colored water rise, pop, and fall back down.
Ask why: the tablet makes carbon dioxide bubbles that carry water upward; when bubbles pop, gravity pulls the water back.
When the fizzing stops, cap the bottle — it becomes a permanent (if sleepy) decoration. Add another half-tablet to wake it up.
summary: Oil, water, and fizzing tablets become a working lava lamp — and a perfect demo of density and gas.
tips: Break tablets in halves — a whole tablet erupts too fast. Dark food coloring shows up best against the oil.
title: DIY Lava Lamps

instructions: Each team gets a raw egg and a 'budget' of materials: straws, tape, cotton balls, newspaper, a paper bag.
Design and build a container that will protect the egg from a 10-foot drop. 20 minutes, no peeking inside after sealing.
Before the drop, each team predicts: survive or scramble? Write it down.
Drop from a stairwell, balcony, or playground structure (adult handles the dropping).
Open the containers. Survivors get glory; scrambled eggs get a redesign round with the leftover budget.
summary: Design a crash-proof container for a raw egg, then drop it from ten feet. Physics decides who wins.
tips: Do the drop over a tarp. The redesign round teaches more than the first build — protect time for it.
title: Egg Drop Challenge

instructions: Pour 1/2 cup of clear or white glue into a bowl and stir in 1/2 teaspoon of baking soda.
Add food coloring and glitter if you want — this is the customization phase.
Add 1 tablespoon of contact lens solution and stir. Keep stirring until it pulls away from the bowl.
Knead with your hands for 2 minutes. Sticky? Add solution a few drops at a time.
Experiment round: split your slime and test add-ins — a spoonful of water (stretchier), cornstarch (stiffer). Record what changes.
Cleanup rule: slime stays at the table, hands get washed, clothes get checked.
summary: Mix the classic polymer slime, then run real experiments: what does water do? Cornstarch? Record the results.
tips: Contact lens solution must list boric acid or sodium borate or it won't work. Aprons or old shirts are non-negotiable.
title: Slime Chemistry Lab

instructions: Draw a simple card design on cardstock — a house with a glowing window, a rocket with a lit flame.
On the inside, map the circuit: draw the path from battery to LED to battery, marking + and −.
Lay copper tape along your drawn path, folding it around corners (never overlapping the two lines).
Tape the LED's legs to the copper tape — long leg to the + line. Tape the coin battery at the other end with the + side matching.
Press to complete the circuit. If it doesn't light, check: battery direction? Tape touching both legs? Lines accidentally crossing?
Decorate the front so the LED shines through a cut-out window.
summary: Build a real working circuit into a greeting card — copper tape, a coin battery, and an LED that actually lights up.
tips: The #1 failure is the LED's legs touching each other — keep them spread. Test the LED on the battery before taping anything.
title: Paper Circuit Greeting Cards
